name: Gnosticism
era: 1st to 4th centuries CE, with living descendants
line: Seek, question the given and look for the light within.

quote.text: If you bring forth what is within you, what you bring forth will save you. If you do not bring forth what is within you, what you do not bring forth will destroy you.

quotes.text: Those who seek should not stop seeking until they find.
For I am the first and the last. I am the honored one and the scorned one.
quotes.source: Nag Hammadi Codex VI, trans. after George MacRae

quotes.text: Who we were, what we have become; where we were, where we were placed; where we are hastening, from what we are redeemed; what birth is, and what rebirth.
quotes.source: Excerpts of Theodotus 78, preserved by Clement of Alexandria; trans. varies

quotes.text: The Son of Man is within you. Follow after him.
quotes.source: Berlin Codex, trans. after R. McL. Wilson and George MacRae

words.meaning: Knowledge by direct insight, not by information
words.usage: The word at the centre of the movements. Salvation was understood as knowing who one is and where one comes from.

words.meaning: Fullness; the divine realm of the aeons
words.usage: The world of light before and above the lower world.

words.meaning: Emptiness; the lower, deficient realm
words.usage: The counterpart of pleroma in some Valentinian texts.

words.meaning: An age; a divine being emanating from the source
words.usage: In many systems the aeons are pairs of divine powers that unfold from the One.

words.meaning: Wisdom; the aeon whose fall begins the story
words.usage: In many myths the youngest aeon who acts without her partner and brings about the world.

words.meaning: The craftsman; the lesser creator of the material world
words.usage: A word from Plato’s Timaeus, used by many texts for the maker of the cosmos.

words.meaning: A name of the lesser creator in Sethian texts
words.usage: The ignorant ruler who claims to be the only god. The origin of the name is debated.
words.language: Aramaic or Hebrew, in Greek texts

words.meaning: A ruler; one of the powers that govern the world
words.usage: In many texts, the rulers who hold souls in the world.

words.meaning: Spirit; breath
words.usage: In Valentinian thought the highest part of a person.

words.meaning: Soul; life breath
words.usage: The middle part of the person in a threefold scheme.

words.meaning: Matter
words.usage: The lowest part, bound to the body.

words.meaning: Word; reason
words.usage: The divine word through which things are known or made.

words.meaning: The first emanation of the divine source in Sethian texts
words.usage: The divine mother or first thought. The origin of the name is unknown.

words.meaning: Thought; insight
words.usage: In the Apocryphon of John a power of light that helps Adam awaken.

words.meaning: A secret writing
words.usage: As in the Apocryphon of John, the "secret book" of John.

words.meaning: The Egyptian town near which thirteen codices were found in 1945
words.usage: The source of most of what we now read directly by gnostic writers.

words.meaning: A book made of folded sheets, not a scroll
words.usage: The form of the Nag Hammadi books, bound in leather.

words.meaning: The last stage of the Egyptian language, written in Greek letters
words.usage: The language of the Nag Hammadi library translations.

words.meaning: Followers of the teacher Valentinus
words.usage: A school that stayed close to ordinary Christian life.

words.meaning: A school that revered Seth, son of Adam
words.usage: The tradition behind the Apocryphon of John, a modern scholarly label.

words.meaning: A follower of an existing Gnostic religion of Iraq and Iran
words.usage: From manda, "knowledge" in Mandaic. A community that continues today.

words.meaning: A follower of the prophet Mani
words.usage: A dualist religion that once stretched from Rome to China.

words.meaning: The writing of opponents against "heresies"
words.usage: Most of what we knew about gnostics before 1945 came from their hostile critics.

words.meaning: A choice; a school of thought
words.usage: The root of "heresy". It first meant a philosophical school, not a wrong belief.

words.meaning: The view that Christ only seemed to have a body
words.usage: A belief ascribed to some gnostic groups.

words.meaning: A flowing out from a source
words.usage: How the divine realms arise from the One, as light from a lamp.

words.meaning: A view with two opposed principles
words.usage: Light and dark, spirit and matter. Not all gnostic systems were dualist in the same way.

words.meaning: A Valentinian image of union with the divine
words.usage: A sacrament or symbol in the Gospel of Philip.

words.meaning: The Human; the primal human being
words.usage: A divine image of the human found in several myths.

words.meaning: A short teaching ascribed to Jesus
words.usage: The Gospel of Thomas is a collection of 114 of them.

words.meaning: Third son of Adam and Eve, a hero of Sethian texts
words.usage: Seen as the ancestor of a line that carries the divine spark.

words.meaning: A disciple of Jesus, prominent in several gnostic gospels
words.usage: In the Gospel of Mary she teaches the other disciples.

practices.name: Seek until you find
practices.instructions: Write one question you are living with on a card. Make it a real one, such as what is mine to do, or what am I afraid of. Sit with it for five minutes without answering. Then write what comes to mind in a few lines. Do not hurry to a conclusion. Repeat the same question each morning for the length of the Onda and see how it changes.
practices.why: The Gospel of Thomas begins by saying that one who seeks must not stop until they find. Treating a question as a companion, not a problem to dispose of, is the heart of the practice.
variations: Choose a different question each day.
Ask it aloud to a friend and listen to theirs.
Write the question on a stone or card and keep it with you.

practices.name: Stillness and light
practices.instructions: Sit comfortably in a dim room. Close your eyes or look softly at a single candle or window. Imagine, without forcing it, a small light in the centre of your chest. Do not try to make it bigger. Stay with it, and when thoughts take you, return. At the end, say to yourself quietly: this is where I come from. Then open your eyes.
practices.why: Many gnostic texts speak of a spark of light within the person that comes from the divine source. A practice of quiet attention is a safe and old way to meet the idea.
variations: Do it outdoors at dawn.
Say a line from Thomas or Thunder, Perfect Mind in place of the closing sentence.
Write a line afterwards on what you saw.

practices.name: A saying at sunrise
practices.instructions: Read one saying from the Gospel of Thomas aloud, slowly, and again, without comment. Then sit for a minute. Do not look for the right interpretation; let it work on you. The sayings were meant to be heard and pondered, not skimmed. Carry the saying with you for the morning, and notice when it comes back.
practices.why: The Gospel of Thomas is a collection of 114 sayings found at Nag Hammadi. Many are short, strange and arresting. They were designed to be turned over, like a stone in the hand.
variations: Read it aloud to someone.
Choose a saying at random.
Write it on a card and put it where you will see it.

practices.name: Write the dream
practices.instructions: Before the day takes over, write down whatever you remember from the night: a dream, a fragment, a feeling. Do it before you check anything. Many modern readers connect gnostic ideas with inner work, and the dream is the most direct material you have. Leave the interpretation for later. The writing is enough.
practices.why: Gnostic writings are full of visions and dreams, and later readers such as Jung read them as the first psychology of the inner world. A dream journal is a simple way of attending to it.
variations: Draw the main image.
Give the dream a title.
Look at the dreams of a week at once.

practices.name: What I do not know
practices.instructions: Look at the sky, or out of a window, and name three things you do not know: about the world, about yourself, about someone near you. Say them without anxiety. This is the opposite of false certainty, and one of the rules of this Onda is to claim no certainty about what is unknown. Notice how roomy it feels.
practices.why: Gnostic texts often speak of a seeker who finds that what they thought they knew was not true. An honest list of what you do not know is a good place to begin to look.
variations: Do it with a friend and compare.
Add one thing you used to think you knew.
Make it a daily list.

practices.name: Go to the source
practices.instructions: Choose a claim you have heard about the Gnostics, or about anything, and go to the source: find the text itself, not a summary or a video. Read a page of the original or the best translation you can find. Notice what it says that the summary did not. One rule of this Onda is to read the sources, not the summaries.
practices.why: The Nag Hammadi find in 1945 meant that for the first time scholars could read Gnostic writings in their own words, instead of through hostile reports. Going to the source is the lesson of the whole discovery.
variations: Look for the original of a famous quote.
Read a primary source for ten minutes.
Ask what the summary left out.

practices.name: Question the given
practices.instructions: Choose one thing you have always taken for granted: a rule, a belief, a habit, a story about yourself. Write it as a sentence. Underneath, write three questions about it: Who told me this? What would I lose if it were false? What would I see if I looked elsewhere? Do not decide anything today; only look.
practices.why: Many Gnostic texts treat seeking and questioning as the beginning of knowledge, and treat what is simply handed down with suspicion.
variations: Do it with a belief about someone else.
Ask a friend the same three questions.
Revisit it a week later.

practices.name: What is within
practices.instructions: Set aside fifteen minutes for something that is within you and rarely comes out: a sketch, a paragraph, a song, a letter you will not send. Do it without an audience and without a purpose. Stop when the time is up. Afterwards write a line on what it felt like to bring it forth and what it might mean to keep it back.
practices.why: Saying 70 of the Gospel of Thomas says that what you bring forth will save you and what you do not will destroy you. Whether read as religion or psychology, it is a bracing thought.
variations: Do it with your non-dominant hand.
Write it and burn or delete it.
Show it to one trusted person.

practices.name: Honour the body
practices.instructions: Do one kind thing for your body right now: stretch, drink water, stand in the sun, eat something good, take a short walk. Treat the body and the world with respect. Many Gnostic writers were wary of matter, but this Onda’s rule is to be gentle with it. The body is where you are, and a decent host.
practices.why: Some Gnostic sources despised the body, others did not. This Onda’s rule is respect: you cannot seek anything well if you neglect the place you are seeking from.
variations: Walk for ten minutes.
Stretch for ten minutes.
Cook yourself a proper meal.

practices.name: Say I do not know
practices.instructions: Today, say I do not know aloud three times, in situations where you would normally bluff or guess. In a meeting, in a conversation, in your own head. Notice how it feels. It is a sign of the seeker, not of weakness. Honesty about the edges of knowledge is the other side of wanting to know more.
practices.why: The Gnostic seeker begins from not knowing. In many texts the first step is the shock of recognising ignorance. Saying so aloud is a mild and useful form of it.
variations: Say it to a child and let them teach you.
Say it to yourself in the mirror.
Say it and then ask a good question.

practices.name: Study a stranger subject
practices.instructions: Pick a subject you know nothing about and spend twenty minutes learning the basics: a language, a craft, a plant, a period of history. Read, watch, or ask. Notice the excitement of beginning from zero. Sophia, wisdom, in Gnostic myth is the one who wanted to know more than she was given. Follow her, gently.
practices.why: Sophia is the figure of Wisdom in many Gnostic myths. Her longing to know is the beginning of the story. Real study is the daily version of that longing.
variations: Learn ten words of a language.
Learn about a tree outside your window.
Ask someone to teach you something they love.

practices.name: Look for the light in someone
practices.instructions: Think of one person you find difficult and try to see the light in them: the spark of what they are at their best, or what they might once have been. Say it to yourself in a sentence. Do not excuse what they do. Only look. It is a way of practising the idea that everyone carries a spark.
practices.why: The idea that each person holds a spark of the divine is one of the warmest in Gnostic thought. It does not remove the need for judgment, but it makes you a better judge.
variations: Do it for a family member.
Do it for a public figure.
Do it for yourself on a hard day.

practices.name: Who, whence and whither
practices.instructions: Take the old Valentinian questions and answer them in a notebook, a line each: Who were we? What have we become? Where were we, and where have we been placed? Where are we hastening? From what are we redeemed? What is birth, and what is rebirth? Do not try to answer all in one night. Pick one each evening and write for ten minutes.
practices.why: The Valentinians summed up gnosis as knowing who we were, what we have become, where we are heading and from what we are released. The questions work as a nightly compass, even without the theology.
variations: Answer in a letter to yourself in ten years.
Discuss one with a friend.
Draw a map of your own answer.

practices.name: Light a candle in a dark room
practices.instructions: Turn off the lights in a room, light a single candle, and sit with it for ten minutes. Look at the flame, then at the dark around it. Think of the small light in the dark as an image of what the Gnostic texts call the spark. Do not try to feel anything in particular. Just sit, and then blow it out.
practices.why: A single flame in the dark is the simplest picture of the spark of light in the Gnostic imagination. It needs no belief, and it is quietly beautiful.
variations: Do it outdoors on a still night.
Do it with a friend in silence.
Write one line afterward.

practices.name: Read a paradox poem
practices.instructions: Read a few lines of Thunder, Perfect Mind, the Nag Hammadi poem in which a divine voice speaks in paradoxes: I am the first and the last, the honoured and the scorned. Read slowly and aloud. Let the contradictions stand without trying to resolve them. Notice what they do in the body, in your breath.
practices.why: Thunder, Perfect Mind is among the most startling texts from Nag Hammadi, a poem in a woman’s voice that sets opposite things side by side. It is made to be heard.
variations: Read it aloud to someone.
Write your own set of paradoxes in the same voice.
Listen to a musical setting.

practices.name: What I forgot
practices.instructions: Ask yourself what you have forgotten today: a promise, a person, a part of yourself. Write one thing. The old Gnostic myths speak of a forgetting from which the soul wakes. In plain terms, ask what you let slip, and see whether it can be picked up tomorrow. Remember one thing, and say so.
practices.why: Waking from forgetfulness is a central Gnostic image: the seeker remembers who they are and where they come from. An evening question about what you have forgotten is a modest, practical form of it.
variations: Ask a friend what you forgot to tell them.
Write a note to your future self.
Remember a person you have lost touch with and write to them.

practices.name: Walk at dusk
practices.instructions: Walk at dusk for twenty minutes and ask: what here belongs to the world, and what belongs to me? Notice the buildings, the trees, the people, your own thoughts. Sort them, loosely, in your mind. Do not decide that the world is bad or good. Only notice where you end and it begins. Come home to a lit room.
practices.why: The Gnostic writers asked what belongs to the world and what to the self, often sharply. A dusk walk puts the question gently and in the open air.
variations: Do it with a friend.
Do it in a place you know well.
Do it in the rain.

practices.name: Where did I claim too much?
practices.instructions: Look back over the day and find one place where you claimed more certainty than you had: a statement of fact, a prediction, a judgment of someone. Write it down, then rewrite it honestly. This Onda’s rule is to claim no certainty about what is unknown. Notice how lightly you can hold a view and still hold it.
practices.why: Gnostic texts are full of claims about the unseen, and their critics were suspicious of them. Checking your own claims at night is the useful side of that suspicion.
variations: Rewrite a text message you regret.
Choose one opinion and rate your confidence from one to ten.
Say sorry to someone you were too sure with.

practices.name: A night of questions
practices.instructions: Invite a friend for an evening of real questions. Each of you brings three, the kind with no easy answer: what do we owe to the dead? What would I be if no one were watching? Take turns. The rule is to ask, listen and wonder; no one has to win. End by choosing one question each to carry for a week.
practices.why: The Gnostic texts are dialogues and questions at heart. A night spent asking and not answering is a very old pleasure, and the best kind of company.
variations: Do it by phone.
Do it as a walk.
Write the questions down for next time.

practices.name: An hour with old manuscripts
practices.instructions: Spend an hour looking at digitised manuscripts online: the Nag Hammadi codices, the Codex Tchacos, any Coptic or Greek papyri from a museum or library. Look at the hands, the margins, the repairs. Let the sense of looking at something made by hand, long ago, quiet your mind. Choose one page and look at it for ten minutes.
practices.why: The Nag Hammadi codices were found in a sealed jar in 1945 and are now in the Coptic Museum in Cairo. Many are online. Looking at them is a way of seeing the hands that copied the words.
variations: Compare two scripts.
Try copying one line of Coptic.
Find the same text in a translation.

immersePlan.name: Read a short text from Nag Hammadi
immersePlan.text: Open the Meyer volume and read a short text, such as Thunder, Perfect Mind, or the Gospel of Truth. Read it slowly. Note one image that stays with you.

immersePlan.name: Read ten sayings of Thomas
immersePlan.text: Read ten sayings from Marvin Meyer’s translation of the Gospel of Thomas. Pick the one that bothers you, and the one that comforts you, and say why.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of The Gnostic Gospels
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Elaine Pagels’s book on how the Nag Hammadi find changed ideas about early Christianity. Notice what you did not know.

immersePlan.name: Watch The Gospel of Judas
immersePlan.text: Watch the National Geographic documentary about the discovery, restoration and meaning of the Codex Tchacos. Notice how long it took to piece the pages back together.

immersePlan.name: Watch The Matrix with Gnostic eyes
immersePlan.text: Watch the film or part of it, as scholars have noted gnostic themes in it: a false world, a hidden truth, an awakening. Notice which choice you would make.

immersePlan.name: Watch Dark City
immersePlan.text: Watch the film in which a man wakes in a city that changes while its people sleep. It is often discussed alongside gnostic themes. Notice who made the world, and what the hero does about it.

immersePlan.name: Listen to In Our Time on Gnosticism
immersePlan.text: Put on the programme in which three scholars discuss who the Gnostics were, what the Nag Hammadi find changed, and why the word is now disputed. Note one idea that you want to look into.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Thunder Perfect Mind
immersePlan.text: Play the album named after the Nag Hammadi poem, and read the poem itself first. Notice how the music approaches the paradoxes.

immersePlan.name: Listen to an episode on the Gnostics
immersePlan.text: Play an episode of Earl Fontainelle’s careful podcast on the Gnostics, or on Valentinus. Listen on a walk, and note one name to look up.

immersePlan.name: Look at an Abraxas gem
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the small engraved stones showing a figure with a rooster’s head and snake legs. Ask what a person wearing one might have wanted it to do.

immersePlan.name: Look at Blake’s Ancient of Days
immersePlan.text: Look at William Blake’s frontispiece of a figure measuring the world with compasses. Many see it as Blake’s image of the lesser creator. Ask what you think he is making.

immersePlan.name: Look at a Nag Hammadi page
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of a page of Codex II, the leather-bound papyrus book that contains the Gospel of Thomas. Look at the handwriting, and imagine who copied it.

immersePlan.name: Eat bread and olives
immersePlan.text: Lay out bread and olives and eat slowly, with nothing else going on. It is the plain fare of late antique Egypt, where the Nag Hammadi books were copied.

immersePlan.name: Cook a lentil stew
immersePlan.text: Cook lentils with onion and olive oil, slowly. It was the staple of ordinary Mediterranean households. Eat it hot, with bread, and think of the scribes eating the same.

immersePlan.name: Eat a fig slowly
immersePlan.text: Eat a fresh or dried fig slowly. Notice the seeds, the sweetness and the texture. A small pleasure to go with a book.

immersePlan.name: Drink a glass of water slowly
immersePlan.text: Drink a glass of plain cool water and attend to it: temperature, taste, the feeling of swallowing. It is the simplest drink there is.

immersePlan.name: Mix wine and water
immersePlan.text: If you drink wine, mix it half with water and drink it slowly. If not, mix grape juice with water. In the ancient Mediterranean wine was always diluted.

immersePlan.name: Make barley water
immersePlan.text: Boil pearl barley in water, cool and strain, and add a squeeze of lemon. A gentle drink for a quiet evening of reading.

immersePlan.name: Sit with one question
immersePlan.text: Choose a question and sit with it for ten minutes, with no need to answer. The gnostic texts treat seeking as a practice, not a stage to get over.

immersePlan.name: Read one saying aloud
immersePlan.text: Read one saying from Thomas, or a poem of your choice, aloud, slowly. The sayings were meant to be heard and pondered, not skimmed.

immersePlan.name: Light a candle in a dark room
immersePlan.text: Turn off the lights, light one candle and sit with it for a few minutes. It is a simple image of the spark of light in the dark.

immersePlan.name: Play The Talos Principle
immersePlan.text: Play a few puzzles of the game in which a voice calling itself your maker sets you tasks in a garden of ruins. Notice what you start to ask about it.

immersePlan.name: Look up Xenogears
immersePlan.text: Xenogears is a long science-fiction epic built on Gnostic themes: a false god, a sleeping memory, a hero who has to ask what he is. Read a short summary or watch a clip.

immersePlan.name: Play Carcassonne
immersePlan.text: Play the tile-laying board game in which you build the walled towns and roads of the Languedoc, the land of the Cathars. Notice how the map grows by many small choices.

immersePlan.name: Keep the feast of Mary Magdalene
immersePlan.text: On 22 July, the feast of Mary Magdalene, whom several texts found at Nag Hammadi present as the disciple who understood. Read a few lines of the Gospel of Mary, and think of what it means to understand.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Coptic Museum
immersePlan.text: Look up the Coptic Museum in Old Cairo, home of the Nag Hammadi codices. Read a short account of how they were found, and look at a photograph of the jar.

immersePlan.name: Remember Montségur
immersePlan.text: On 16 March, in 1244, more than two hundred Cathars who would not recant were burned below the castle of Montségur. Read a short account, and spend a quiet minute thinking of people who kept to a belief at a cost.

immersePlan.name: Think about gnosis
immersePlan.text: Gnosis is knowledge by direct insight, not by being told. Choose one thing you know only because you were told, and one you know because you saw it. Write both. Notice the difference.

immersePlan.name: Think about Sophia
immersePlan.text: Sophia is Wisdom, the aeon whose longing to know begins the story. Think of the last time you wanted to know something badly enough to follow it. Do one more step toward it today.

immersePlan.name: Think about the pleroma
immersePlan.text: Pleroma is fullness, the divine realm of light. Think of a moment when you felt completely full of something, such as joy, attention or love. Write three lines about where you were, and what you were doing.

rules.text: Keep seeking and do not rest in borrowed answers
rules.why: The mood of the Gospel of Thomas is questioning. A belief you have tested is worth more than one you inherited.

rules.text: Read the sources, not just the summaries
rules.why: Our idea of the gnostics was shaped for centuries by their critics. Go to the texts and to modern scholars.

rules.text: Do not claim certainty about what is unknown
rules.why: The texts are fragmentary and the movements varied. Hold your conclusions loosely, and say “I don’t know” out loud.

rules.text: Treat the body and the world with respect
rules.why: Some texts despised the world, but others did not, and ordinary life is where the practice happens. Do not use these ideas to despise yourself.

rules.text: Pay attention to what is within you
rules.why: The tradition keeps returning to an inner source. Give it a few minutes a day.

rules.text: Beware of secret knowledge sold as a shortcut
rules.why: Gnostic teaching was never a quick trick. Be suspicious of anyone who promises hidden truth for a fee.

read.title: The Nag Hammadi Scriptures
read.creator: Edited by Marvin Meyer
read.why: The principal Nag Hammadi texts in a single accessible English volume.

read.title: The Gnostic Gospels
read.creator: Elaine Pagels
read.why: A well-known book that explains how the Nag Hammadi find changed ideas of early Christianity. It won the National Book Award.

read.title: What Is Gnosticism?
read.creator: Karen L. King
read.why: A rigorous critique of the category and a history of the term.

read.title: The Gnostic Religion
read.creator: Hans Jonas
read.why: A philosophical classic that sets gnosticism beside modern existentialism.

read.title: Rethinking "Gnosticism"
read.creator: Michael Allen Williams
read.why: Argues that the category should be dropped, and replaced with more precise terms.

read.title: The Gospel of Thomas: The Hidden Sayings of Jesus
read.creator: Marvin Meyer
read.why: A translation of all 114 sayings with commentary.

read.title: The Gospel of Judas
read.creator: Rodolphe Kasser, Marvin Meyer and Gregor Wurst
read.why: The first publication of a text found in the Codex Tchacos, with essays.

read.title: Beyond Belief: The Secret Gospel of Thomas
read.creator: Elaine Pagels
read.why: A reading of Thomas and John side by side.

watch.title: The Gospel of Judas
watch.creator: National Geographic
watch.why: A documentary on the discovery, restoration and meaning of the Codex Tchacos.

watch.title: The Matrix
watch.creator: The Wachowskis
watch.why: A film about a false world and awakening. Scholars have noted gnostic echoes. It is a modern work and not a source.

watch.title: Dark City
watch.creator: Alex Proyas
watch.why: A film in which a man wakes in a city that changes while its people sleep, and slowly learns who made it. Often discussed alongside gnostic themes of a false world and awakening.

listen.title: In Our Time: Gnosticism
listen.creator: BBC Radio 4, Melvyn Bragg
listen.why: Three scholars on who the Gnostics were, what the Nag Hammadi find changed, and why the word itself is now disputed.

listen.title: Thunder Perfect Mind
listen.creator: Current 93
listen.why: An album named after the Nag Hammadi poem in which a divine voice speaks in paradoxes. Listen after reading the poem itself.

listen.title: The Secret History of Western Esotericism Podcast
listen.creator: Earl Fontainelle
listen.why: A long, careful series by a scholar. The episodes on the Gnostics and on Valentinus interview the people who edit the texts.

art.title: Abraxas gems
art.creator: Craftsmen of the Roman Empire
art.why: Small engraved stones showing a figure with a rooster’s head and snake legs, named Abraxas. Many are in museum collections.

art.title: The Ancient of Days
art.creator: William Blake
art.why: A frontispiece showing a figure measuring the world with compasses. Many readers see in it a lesser creator.

art.title: Codex II of Nag Hammadi
art.creator: Coptic scribes
art.why: A leather-bound papyrus book that contains the Gospel of Thomas, kept in the Coptic Museum in Cairo.

eat.title: Bread and olives
eat.creator: Plain fare of late antique Egypt
eat.why: The everyday food of the Egypt where the Nag Hammadi books were copied. Eat slowly, with nothing else going on.

eat.title: Lentil stew
eat.creator: A plain pot
eat.why: Lentils with onion and olive oil, the staple of ordinary Mediterranean households in late antiquity. Eat it hot, with bread.

eat.title: Figs
eat.creator: Fruit of the eastern Mediterranean
eat.why: A fruit eaten fresh and dried in the ancient Mediterranean. A small pleasure to eat while you read.

drink.title: Water
drink.creator: Plain and cool
drink.why: The simplest drink and the clearest image of what runs through many ancient texts. Drink a glass slowly and attend to it.

drink.title: Wine mixed with water
drink.creator: A late antique custom
drink.why: Wine was usually drunk diluted in the ancient Mediterranean. Non-drinkers can mix grape juice and water the same way.

drink.title: Barley water
drink.creator: A plain drink
drink.why: Boiled barley, cooled and strained, a gentle non-alcoholic drink of the ancient Mediterranean. Good for a quiet evening.

customs.title: Sit with a question
customs.creator: No answer needed
customs.why: The gnostic texts treat seeking as a practice, not a stage to get over.

customs.title: Keep a dream journal
customs.creator: Write before the day takes over
customs.why: Many modern readers connect gnostic ideas with inner work. Jung wrote on them.

customs.title: Read one saying aloud
customs.creator: From Thomas, or a poem of your choice
customs.why: The sayings were meant to be heard and pondered, not skimmed.

customs.title: Light a candle in a dark room
customs.creator: And sit for a few minutes
customs.why: A simple image of the spark of light in the dark.

games.title: Xenogears
games.creator: Video game · Square
games.why: A long science-fiction epic built on Gnostic themes: a false god, a sleeping humanity and knowledge as the way out.

games.title: The Talos Principle
games.creator: Video game · Croteam
games.why: A voice calling itself your maker sets you puzzles in a garden and forbids one tower. The question of whether to obey it is the game.

games.title: Carcassonne
games.creator: Board game · Klaus-Jürgen Wrede
games.why: Tile by tile you build the walled towns and roads of the Languedoc, the country of the Cathars. A light way into the landscape.

festivals.title: Parwanaya
festivals.creator: Five days in spring
festivals.why: The great festival of the Mandaeans, the one Gnostic religion that has survived from antiquity. It is kept with baptisms in running water.

festivals.title: Dehwa Rabba
festivals.creator: Midsummer
festivals.why: The Mandaean New Year. Families stay indoors for a day and a half while, in their tradition, the guardian spirits are away.

festivals.title: Feast of Mary Magdalene
festivals.creator: 22 July
festivals.why: Several texts found at Nag Hammadi present her as the disciple who understood most.

festivals.title: Montségur remembered
festivals.creator: 16 March
festivals.why: On this day in 1244 more than two hundred Cathars who refused to recant were burned below their mountain fortress.

places.title: Coptic Museum
places.creator: Old Cairo, Egypt
places.why: Home of the Nag Hammadi codices, the leather-bound books found in a jar in 1945. Pages are on display.

places.title: Montségur
places.creator: Ariège, France
places.why: A steep walk to the ruined castle on its rock, and a memorial stone in the field below.

places.title: Museum of Catharism
places.creator: Mazamet, Tarn, France
places.why: A clear account of what the Cathars believed and how they were destroyed.

places.title: Chester Beatty
places.creator: Dublin, Ireland
places.why: The library holds rare Manichaean papyri in Coptic from Egypt, with some on show.

places.title: Cao’an
places.creator: Jinjiang, Fujian, China
places.why: A stone hut on a hillside with a carved image of Mani as the Buddha of Light. It is the last Manichaean temple still standing.

ethics.title: Seek, and do not stop
ethics.text: The Gospel of Thomas says that the seeker should not stop until they find, and that finding brings trouble and wonder. The ethic is sustained honesty about what you do not yet know.
ethics.practice: Name one thing you have stopped questioning, and question it kindly.

ethics.title: Compassion toward the whole person
ethics.text: The Valentinian and Mary texts often speak of care for others as the visible fruit of knowledge. Insight that does not soften the heart is empty.
ethics.practice: Do one kind thing for someone with whom you disagree.

ethics.title: Freedom from compulsion
ethics.text: Many texts describe the soul as held by powers that bind it: fate, desire, fear. Knowledge is meant to loosen them.
ethics.practice: Name one habit that binds you and take one small step out of it.

ethics.title: Humility about hidden things
ethics.text: Because the texts are partial and the movements varied, the honest response is humility. No one has the full account.
ethics.practice: Say "I do not know" once today.

ethics.title: Do not despise the body
ethics.text: Opponents accused gnostics of hating the body, and some texts do. Others honour the body as the place of awakening. Care for your body is part of attention.
ethics.practice: Spend ten minutes caring for your body: stretch, wash, rest.

ethics.title: Honest speech
ethics.text: In the Gospel of Mary the Saviour tells the disciples not to lay down rules beyond what has been given. A teacher who imposes more than they have lived deserves suspicion.
ethics.practice: Speak only from what you know today.

philosophy.title: The spark within
philosophy.text: Many texts speak of a spark of divine light in the person, a part that remembers where it came from. The idea is that a person is more than their circumstances, and that the self is not wholly made by the world.
philosophy.practice: Ask what in you feels older than your history.

philosophy.title: A flawed world
philosophy.text: Some texts say that the world was made by an ignorant or lesser power and is therefore flawed. The thought answers an old question: why is there suffering? It need not mean that the world is evil, only that it is incomplete.
philosophy.practice: Look at one flaw in the world and ask what it calls you to repair.

philosophy.title: Sophia’s story
philosophy.text: In many myths Wisdom, the youngest aeon, acts without her partner and falls into confusion, from which the lower world arises. Her story is also one of longing, and of restoration.
philosophy.practice: Think of a time when acting alone brought confusion, and what restored you.

philosophy.title: Knowledge that saves
philosophy.text: For the gnostics salvation is not obedience or good works alone but knowing one’s true origin and nature. The word gnosis means direct acquaintance, as with a person, rather than facts.
philosophy.practice: Think of the difference between knowing about someone and knowing them.

philosophy.title: Seeking and finding
philosophy.text: Saying 2 of Thomas describes a progress: seek, find, be troubled, marvel, reign, rest. It is a pattern of inner discovery that includes distress.
philosophy.practice: Where are you in the sequence?

philosophy.title: The paradoxes of the Perfect Mind
philosophy.text: Thunder, Perfect Mind is a poem in which a feminine voice says "I am the honoured one and the scorned one" and many other opposites. It insists that the divine is not captured by one side.
philosophy.practice: Write four lines of "I am" with opposites that are both true of you.

philosophy.title: The inward kingdom
philosophy.text: In Thomas, Jesus says that the kingdom is inside you and outside you, and that those who know themselves will be known. The place of the sacred is shifted from temple to self.
philosophy.practice: Find a moment today when the outer and the inner felt connected.

philosophy.title: Many gnosticisms
philosophy.text: Modern scholars stress that there was no single gnostic church. Valentinians, Sethians, followers of Thomas, Marcion and Manichaeans differed deeply. A careful approach speaks of particular groups.
philosophy.practice: When you read about gnostics, ask which group is meant.

philosophy.title: The voice of the losers
philosophy.text: Early Christian writers such as Irenaeus attacked gnostic teachers as heretics, and most of their books were destroyed. The Nag Hammadi finds gave their voices back. History is written by winners, and sometimes rewritten.
philosophy.practice: Read one account of an event from the point of view of a group that lost.

philosophy.title: Mandaeans today
philosophy.text: The Mandaeans, a small community of Iraq and Iran with diaspora communities worldwide, are the one gnostic religion that has lasted to the present. They honour John the Baptist and baptise often in flowing water. Their existence is a reminder that gnostic ideas are a living inheritance for some.
philosophy.practice: Learn one fact about the Mandaeans from a Mandaean source.

intro: Gnosticism is a modern name for a range of religious movements of the first centuries CE that stressed gnosis, direct knowledge of the divine and of oneself, as the way of salvation. The word comes from the Greek for knowledge. There was never a single gnostic church. Teachers such as Valentinus and Basilides founded schools in Alexandria and Rome, and other groups, called Sethian by scholars, produced texts such as the Secret Book of John.

Until the twentieth century almost everything people knew about these movements came from their opponents, notably Irenaeus of Lyons, whose Against Heresies, written around 180, described and attacked them. This changed in December 1945, when a farmer near the Egyptian town of Nag Hammadi found a sealed jar containing thirteen papyrus codices. They held about fifty-two texts in Coptic, including the Gospel of Thomas, the Gospel of Philip and the Apocryphon of John. For the first time historians could read gnostic authors in their own words.

Many of these texts share a pattern of ideas. A transcendent divine source emanates a realm of light, the pleroma, of paired powers called aeons. The youngest, Sophia, Wisdom, acts without her partner, and from her disturbance a lesser creator arises, often called the Demiurge, who makes the visible world and believes he is the only god. Humans carry a spark of divine light, and a messenger from the realm of light awakens them to remember where they came from. Salvation is that awakening.

Scholars now debate whether "Gnosticism" is a useful category at all. Michael Williams and Karen King have argued that it lumps together very different groups and repeats the polemic of ancient critics. Valentinians remained close to ordinary Christian life. The Gospel of Thomas has no creation myth. Manichaeism, founded by Mani in the third century, was a separate and very successful religion. A careful reading speaks of particular texts and schools.

The tradition did not vanish. The Mandaeans, a community from southern Iraq and Iran now spread across the world, have kept a gnostic religion with its own scriptures and baptisms for nearly two thousand years. Medieval dualist movements such as the Cathars of southern France were sometimes linked to gnostic ideas, though the historical connection is disputed. In the twentieth century, thinkers such as Carl Jung, Hans Jonas and Elaine Pagels renewed interest in the texts.

This Onda uses the questions and images of these texts as invitations to attention. It offers a practice of seeking, of expressing what is within, and of asking who we are, rather than a doctrine. It does not imitate the rites of any group, and it asks you to remember that the Mandaeans are living people with their own voice.
guide.origin: Egypt, Syria, Rome and the wider Mediterranean, and later Iraq and Iran
guide.era: 1st to 4th centuries CE, with living descendants

figures.name: Valentinus
figures.bio: Teacher born in Egypt, who taught in Alexandria and Rome and founded the most influential gnostic school. Little of his own writing survives.

figures.name: Basilides
figures.bio: Alexandrian teacher known mostly through his opponents. His teaching included a vision of a remote, ineffable God.

figures.name: Irenaeus of Lyons
figures.bio: Bishop whose Against Heresies is the main hostile source on gnostic groups. His work is both valuable and partisan.

figures.name: Clement of Alexandria
figures.bio: Christian teacher who used the word gnosis for the higher knowledge of the believer, and preserved Valentinian extracts.

figures.name: Plotinus
figures.bio: Platonist philosopher who wrote against the gnostics in Rome, defending the goodness of the cosmos.

figures.name: Mani
figures.bio: Prophet from Mesopotamia who founded Manichaeism, a religion that spread from North Africa to China.

figures.name: Mary Magdalene
figures.bio: A disciple of Jesus who appears as an important teacher in the Gospel of Mary, the Gospel of Philip and other texts.

figures.name: Hans Jonas
figures.bio: German-American philosopher, author of The Gnostic Religion, who compared the gnostic mood to modern alienation.

figures.name: Elaine Pagels
figures.bio: Historian of religion whose The Gnostic Gospels, 1979, brought the Nag Hammadi texts to a wide audience.

figures.name: Karen L. King
figures.bio: Scholar of early Christianity whose What Is Gnosticism?, 2003, questioned the category.

figures.name: Marvin Meyer
figures.bio: Scholar and translator of the Nag Hammadi texts and the Gospel of Thomas.

history.detail: Ideas about a hidden knowledge, a lesser creator and a spark of light grew out of Jewish, Platonic and early Christian thought in the eastern Mediterranean.
The teacher, born in Egypt, taught in Alexandria and then Rome. He and his followers developed a rich system of aeons and remained within the wider Christian community for some time.
The bishop of Lyons set out to expose gnostic teachings, quoting many of them. His work shaped later views and is the main source before 1945.

history.what: Texts of Thomas, Philip and John
history.detail: The Gospel of Thomas, the Gospel of Philip, the Apocryphon of John and others were composed. They circulated in Greek and Syriac and later in Coptic translation.
The philosopher wrote a treatise criticising a group in his circle for despising the world and its beauty.
Mani, born in Mesopotamia, preached a religion of light and darkness. His movement spread widely and lasted for a thousand years.
In his Easter letter, Athanasius of Alexandria named the twenty-seven books of the New Testament, and condemned other writings. The Nag Hammadi books were probably hidden around this period.

In southern France, a dualist movement was suppressed in the Albigensian Crusade from 1209. The fortress of Montségur fell in 1244. Whether the Cathars were true heirs of ancient gnostics is disputed.
A papyrus book bought in Cairo included the Gospel of Mary and the Secret Book of John. It was not published until 1955.
In December, farmers near Nag Hammadi found a jar with thirteen codices. The circumstances of the discovery are told in several versions.

history.what: The Nag Hammadi Library in English
history.detail: James M. Robinson’s team published the complete translation, which opened the texts to general readers.
A text from the Codex Tchacos was published and restored, showing a Judas who is closer to Jesus than the other disciples.

concepts.detail: The gnostic texts treat knowledge as acquaintance rather than information: knowing one’s source, one’s nature and one’s destiny. It is gained by insight and often by a teacher’s help. It transforms the person who knows.

concepts.text: The fullness of the divine world.
concepts.detail: In many systems the pleroma is made up of aeons, powers that emanate in pairs from an unknowable source. It is the realm of light from which the spark in each person comes and to which it returns. The lower world is outside it.

concepts.text: Wisdom, the aeon whose fall begins the story.
concepts.detail: In several myths she brings forth something without her partner and the result is a flawed being, the maker of the world. In others she is a figure of longing and restoration who is eventually reunited with the fullness.

concepts.text: The lesser creator of the world.
concepts.detail: Taken from Plato’s craftsman in the Timaeus, the Demiurge in Sethian texts is ignorant and arrogant, sometimes called Yaldabaoth. The picture expresses the sense that the world is not as it should be, and that its ruler is not the highest.

Humans, the texts say, carry a portion of the divine that has been forgotten. A messenger awakens them to it. It is not earned but remembered. The idea gives a person a dignity beyond their circumstances.

concepts.text: The flowing out of the divine realms.
concepts.detail: Rather than creating by command, the highest source gives rise to levels of being, as light spreads from a lamp. Each level is a little less perfect. The model is shared with Neoplatonism.

concepts.text: A school close to the Christian community.
concepts.detail: The Valentinians counted spiritual, psychic and material people and held that all could be moved toward gnosis. They used rituals like the bridal chamber and wrote the Gospel of Truth. They stayed within wider Christian life for some time.

The Gospel of Thomas gathers 114 sayings of Jesus without narrative or doctrine. It stresses self-knowledge and the inward kingdom. Many scholars place its composition in the first or second century, and its relation to the other gospels is debated.

Mandaeans revere John the Baptist, perform frequent baptisms in flowing water, and keep a large body of scriptures in Mandaic. Their name comes from manda, knowledge. They have lived in southern Iraq and Iran for centuries and are now spread around the world.
Scholars such as Michael Williams and Karen King argue that the label groups very different movements and reproduces the view of their opponents. A careful reader names the group or text instead.

facts.text: The Nag Hammadi codices were found in December 1945 in a sealed jar by local farmers near the town. The books were bound in leather and written in Coptic.
The Gospel of Thomas consists of 114 sayings of Jesus, with almost no narrative.
The word heresy comes from the Greek hairesis, which at first just meant a choice or a school of thought.
Part of the Gospel of Thomas was known before 1945 from three Greek fragments found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, between 1897 and 1903.
The Mandaeans are one of the world’s oldest surviving gnostic communities, and have a priesthood and large body of religious literature.
The Codex Tchacos, which contains the Gospel of Judas, was found in Egypt in the 1970s and passed through many hands before being restored and published in 2006.
Carl Jung wrote a poetic text in 1916 called Seven Sermons to the Dead, in the voice of the gnostic teacher Basilides.

sensitivity.note: Gnosticism is a modern umbrella term for diverse ancient movements, and the Mandaeans are a living gnostic community. This Onda offers questions, images and attention in a form open to anyone. It does not reproduce the rites of any group.
requiredCaveats: Scholars dispute the word Gnosticism. The texts are fragmentary, the groups differed, and our older picture was drawn by their opponents. Treat sweeping claims, including those in popular books, with care.
The Mandaeans are a living people, and their baptismal and priestly rites belong to them. Learn from Mandaeans themselves.
Gnostic ideas, read in a certain way, can be used to despise the body, other people or the world. This Onda asks you to use them to look inward with care, and to keep the world and the body in view.
